structure.overview: This case concerns the application of the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) to tax avoidance transactions undertaken by DAC Investment Holdings Inc., which continued its incorporation from Canada to the British Virgin Islands to defer tax on investment income. The Crown, as appellant, challenged the Tax Court's decision that found no abuse of the Income Tax Act provisions, arguing that DAC's transactions frustrated the object, spirit, and purpose of anti-deferral tax measures. The Federal Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal, finding that GAAR applies and that DAC's continuance to the BVI constituted an abuse of the relevant tax provisions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: DAC undertook transactions to circumvent tax measures and benefit from tax deferral on a share sale by transferring shares between CCPCs and continuing DAC to the BVI.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: DAC's continuance to the BVI caused it to be deemed incorporated there and no longer a CCPC, enabling tax deferral subject to GAAR application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister reassessed DAC under GAAR and denied the tax deferral.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Tax Court allowed DAC's appeal, and the Crown now appeals to this Court.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court concludes GAAR applies and would allow the Crown's appeal.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Appellant DAC was incorporated in Ontario in 2001, underwent name changes, was controlled by David Civiero, acquired Soberlink shares via rollover, and continued into the BVI in 2015.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: From 2015 to 2019, David Civiero was the sole common shareholder of DAC.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister reassessed DAC under GAAR by increasing tax payable under section 123.3 and denying a deduction under section 123.4.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 123.3 levies refundable tax on CCPC investment income; section 123.4 permits a tax deduction but excludes CCPC investment income from rate reduction.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sections 123.3 and 123.4 collectively prevent tax deferral on investment income earned by a CCPC, called anti-deferral measures.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: DAC conceded tax benefit and two avoidance transactions: rollover of shares and continuance to BVI; main issue was abuse.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Crown argued DAC abused anti-deferral measures and related ITA provisions in the Tax Court.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court determined the object, spirit and purpose of provisions, then assessed abuse.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court rejected Crown's argument that anti-deferral measures apply to all private corporations, limiting them to CCPCs.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court found no abuse as Parliament intended different rules for CCPCs and non-CCPCs, and DAC's move was allowed.
idea_list: DAC's move from CCPC to non-CCPC allowed

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: GAAR analysis involves three steps: tax benefit, avoidance transaction, and abuse; only abuse is at issue here.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Parties agree tax benefit and avoidance transactions exist; only abuse is disputed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Supreme Court says abuse occurs if transactions produce outcomes provisions seek to prevent, defeat rationale, or frustrate purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The issue is whether Tax Court erred in finding the transactions did not frustrate the provisions' object, spirit and purpose.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Tax Court held no abuse because anti-deferral measures apply only to CCPCs and DAC was not a CCPC when gain realized.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court finds Tax Court overstated Parliament's intent; transactions defeat Parliament's objective against tax deferral.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court declines to decide if anti-deferral measures apply beyond CCPCs, leaving that for another case.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Assuming anti-deferral measures apply only to CCPCs, the Court proceeds to analyze abuse issue.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Determining object, spirit and purpose is a legal question reviewed for correctness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 123.3 was enacted in 1995 to increase tax on investment income to prevent deferral through corporations.

summaries.speaker: evidence
summaries.summary: Section 123.3 imposes a refundable tax on CCPCs' investment income at 10 2/3% of lesser of investment income or taxable income excess.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Tax Court described section 123.3's object, spirit and purpose at paragraph 139.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 123.3 addresses the part of the tax scheme aimed at preventing deferral of investment income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 123.3's purpose is to reduce income tax deferral opportunities for individuals earning investment income via CCPCs.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: CCPC investment income benefits from incentivized tax rates and dividend refunds introduced in 1971 reform.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains that investment income earned by a CCPC is excluded from the section 123.4 rate reduction, citing relevant ITA provisions.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court described the object, spirit and purpose of section 123.4 at paragraph 158 of its reasons.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Tax Court used 'general corporate tax rate' to mean a non-incentivized rate and described the legislation but not its rationale.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds that part of the rationale of section 123.4 is to foster international competitiveness for Canadian business, excluding already incentivized rates like CCPC investment income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court notes the Department of Finance aimed to foster competitiveness but also preserved the principle that investment income should be taxed equally whether received directly or through a private corporation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states the object and purpose of excluding CCPC investment income from section 123.4 tax reduction is twofold: preferential tax rate and preserving tax equality principle.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The amendment aimed to make corporate continuances fairer by having residence determine tax liability, avoiding prior unfair taxation results.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court quotes subsection 250(5.1) deeming a corporation incorporated in the new jurisdiction from continuance until any further continuance.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court notes the new regime was ambitious but imperfect, with further revisions needed to improve corporate immigration and continuance rules.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court described the object, spirit and purpose of subsection 250(5.1) in its reasons at paragraph 185.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Tax Court on the amendment's intent but finds it erred by not accurately stating the object, spirit and purpose regarding Parliament's intended results.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states the object, spirit and purpose of subsection 250(5.1) is to make tax provisions fairer for corporations moving into or leaving Canada by continuance.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court outlines the three conditions a corporation must satisfy to be a CCPC: private corporation, Canadian corporation, and Canadian-controlled.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court quotes the definition of CCPC from subsection 125(7), excluding corporations controlled by non-residents or public corporations.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The second stage of abuse analysis asks if the transaction frustrates the object, spirit and purpose of the provisions relied on for the tax benefit.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The second stage abuse analysis is fact-intensive and reviewed for palpable and overriding error unless there is an extricable error of law.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Two avoidance transactions are at issue: share rollover from Jacal to DAC and DAC's continuance into the BVI, with focus on the continuance for abuse analysis.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Tax Court suggests Parliament intended subsection 250(5.1) may be used to circumvent anti-deferral measures, a critical Canadian tax policy.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court supports its conclusion by noting Parliament enacted provisions to facilitate movement from CCPC to non-CCPC status.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the Tax Court erred in law by concluding GAAR cannot apply just because Parliament allows a corporation to cease being a CCPC.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Tax Court found DAC did not abuse provisions because it chose to move from one taxing regime to another with different advantages and disadvantages.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states that theoretical minuses are only relevant if material to DAC in the abuse analysis.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court is not persuaded that DAC was materially adversely affected by longer reassessment periods or that minuses were material.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: DAC acknowledges the transactions were undertaken for tax benefits, making it implausible minuses outweighed pluses.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court concludes pluses and minuses were irrelevant and the Tax Court erred by relying on them to find no abuse.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Tax Court's no-abuse finding cannot stand due to errors and lack of deference owed on subsection 250(5.1) object, spirit and purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court will undertake a fresh analysis of whether the avoidance transactions abuse the relevant provisions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds there was abuse of subsection 250(5.1) because DAC's continuance frustrated the provision's object, spirit and purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: DAC's continuance into the BVI was unrelated to business ties and was virtually inconsequential except for tax benefits, frustrating the provision's purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The use of subsection 250(5.1) was merely a means to achieve tax benefits, which was not the provision's object or purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds that sections 123.3 and 123.4 anti-deferral provisions were abused by the continuance, frustrating their purpose.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Crown that circumventing anti-deferral measures undermines their effectiveness and Parliament did not intend this.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the Tax Court erred and that GAAR applies because the continuance circumvented anti-deferral provisions' rationale.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: DAC argues that if GAAR applies, the reassessment should use a three-year period for CCPCs, making the reassessment statute barred.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states subsection 245(2) of the ITA governs GAAR adjustments to deny tax benefits from avoidance transactions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains subsection 245(2) limits GAAR adjustments to denying tax benefits, rejecting DAC's reassessment period argument.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court concludes section 123.3 aims to prevent CCPCs from deferring taxes payable at higher rates by shareholders, maintaining tax integration.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds section 123.4's purpose is to lower the general corporate tax rate to a maximum 15% non-refundable rate.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains subsection 250(5.1) equates place of continuance with incorporation to ensure proper tax treatment after continuation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states Parliament intended corporations to move jurisdictions, facilitating this with provisions recognizing such moves.
